Here we give a brief overview of our contributions: 48 We introduce and formalize the problem of dynamic necklace splitting. 49 We design a linear-time algorithm for swapping adjacent beads when n= 2that achieves 50 the optimal bound of 2(k−1)cuts. We 52 also design a linear-time algorithm for relocation with looser bounds for general n≥2

Soon after the necklace splitting problem was originally introduced [ 6], Goldberg and West [ 9] 88 proved that a solution always exists if k= 2. Alon and West [ 3] gave a simpler proof using 89 the Borsuk–Ulam theorem [ 7], and Alon [ 1] generalized the results to k>2. Finally, Alon 90 and Graur [ 2] discovered an efficient approximation algorithm for finding a solution with few 91 cuts. Alon and Graur [ 2] also consider an online variation of the problem. They derive lower 92 and upper bounds on the number of cuts needed when k= 2based on the value of n. They 93 also generalize some of these results to the k>2case. 94 In addition to necklace splitting, other fair division problems can be extended to dynamic 95 settings. Kash et al. [ 13] study a fair division problem with divisible goods where agents with 96 Leontiefpreferencesarriveovertimeandgoodsmustbeirrevocablyallocated. In addition to ensuring fairness, such data-informed hash maps can even be faster than 105 traditional hash maps [ 14,17]. Shahbazi et al. [ 19] use the static necklace splitting problem 106 to design hash maps that satisfy group fairness. However, making dynamic updates to these 107 hash maps is infeasible without a dynamic solution to the necklace splitting problem. 108 For a concrete application, consider the use of fair hash maps to maintain user information 109 on a social network. Whenever new users join the network, their data needs to be efficiently 110 added to the hash map, and when users leave, their data needs to be efficiently removed. 111 As users’ attributes change, their data needs to be efficiently updated (corresponding to 112 relocation of beads in a necklace). 113 Another concrete application involves table joins in data lakes. Consider an organization 114 seeking to share its data with third parties. The data is stored in a data lake and includes 115 sensitive information as primary keys for certain tables. To protect user privacy, the data 116 needs to be hashed, which introduces the risk of hash collision. A fair hashing scheme 117 must be used to ensure any resulting errors when joining on the hashed columns do not 118 disproportionately impact a specific demographic group [ 19]. For this system to be efficient, 119 it needs to be easy to update the hashes as the data changes. 120 1.5.2

Consider the problem of load-balancing among multiple servers, where tasks need to be 122 completed in a specific order. Each agent corresponds to a server, and each bead color 123 corresponds to a different type of task. We want to spread the load across the servers evenly, 124 but we also want to minimize communication costs [ 12]. This necessitates having as few cuts 125 as possible. 126 If the order of tasks needs to be modified, new tasks need to be added, or existing tasks 127 need to be canceled, we would want to be able to update the computation plan without 128 recreating it from scratch. As a special case, if computation has already begun, we can 129 still perform dynamic updates that don’t affect the already-completed tasks using dynamic 130 necklace splitting. 131 1.5.3

Another key application is ensuring minority representation in bucketization. For example, 133 when partitioning data for machine learning tasks, it is crucial that the training data is 134 accurately represented by the test data for reliable results [ 18]. Intentionally designing the 135 bucketization process to maintain fairness helps prevent downstream fairness issues [ 15,16]. 136 Here, each agent represents a bucket, and the color of each bead represents the grouping 137 attribute. If the “red” data is more sparse than the “blue” data, it is important that the 138 relative proportions are preserved to have accurate results. 139

paragraph: In the first case, there is a cut to the left of the red bead and to the right of the blue 442 bead (or it is at the end of the necklace). This is the simplest case – we swap the beads and 443 let the agents retain ownership of their original beads. No cuts need to be adjusted. 444 In the second case, there is a cut on the left, but not the right. We swap the beads and do 445 not adjust any cuts. A2takes possession of the left interval, and A1takes possession of the 446 right interval. As part of the right interval, A1gains at least one unneeded extra bead (the 447 green one). Each extra bead lacks a cut to its left, so they must be the first of their colors. 448 Thus, the original beads of A1are somewhere to the right in the necklace. Furthermore, 449 since each of the original beads is not the first of its color, they each start their own intervals. 450 A2takes ownership of each of these intervals and repeats the process with each of them if 451 they have multiple beads, continuing to attempt to re-satisfy the fairness constraint. Since 452 the necklace has exactly n−1pairs of adjacent beads without a cut, this results in at most 453 nownership exchanges throughout the procedure. 454 In the third case, there is no cut on the left. We swap the beads and move the cut left 455 by one bead (to ensure that the set of cuts maintains the structure of one generated by the 456 offline algorithm). A1andA2retain the left and right intervals, respectively. Similarly to 457 the second case, to maintain the fairness constraint, at most n−1intervals will have to be 458 exchanged between the two agents. 459 We will henceforth refer to this procedure as DenseSwap . The two-dimensional array 460 allows us to perform each ownership exchange in constant time, giving a running time of 461 O(n)forDenseSwap . 462 ▶Theorem 15. DenseSwap produces a set of cuts of size exactly n(k−1)and has time 463 complexity O(n). 464 5.2

There are four possible cases. 469 In the first case, the bead to be relocated begins as the first of its color and remains 470 so. We move the bead to the desired position, and if the interval is owned by a different 471 agent, we re-satisfy the fairness constraint by exchanging at most nintervals between the 472 two agents, as in the previous section. 473 In the second case, the bead to be relocated begins not as the first of its color and remains 474 so. We move the bead and its corresponding cut to an arbitrary boundary to make it a 475 singleton interval, and if the two affected intervals are not owned by the same agent, we 476 re-satisfy the fairness constraint by exchanging at most n−1intervals between the two 477 agents. Then, we move the bead and its corresponding cut to the desired position, and if 478 the destination interval does not belong to the owner of the bead, we re-satisfy the fairness 479 constraint by exchanging at most nintervals between the two agents. 480 In the third case, the bead begins as the first of its color but does not remain so. We 481 relocate the bead directly to the left of the second red bead via Case 1, and then we relocate 482 the second red bead to the desired position via Case 2. At most 3n−1intervals are exchanged 483 throughout this case. 484 In the fourth case, the bead begins not as the first of its color but becomes the first. We 485 relocate the bead and its corresponding cut directly to the right of the first red bead via 486 Case 2, and then we relocate the first red bead to the desired position via Case 1. At most 487 3n−1intervals are exchanged throughout this case. 488 We will henceforth refer to this procedure as DenseJump . We now show how to adapt ApproxStatic to the dynamic setting. Our algorithm can handle 550 any type of dynamization, including relocation, insertion, and deletion. 551 Notice that the crux of ApproxStatic relies on a small set of samples (given sufficiently 552 smallk). Hence, if we ensure that sampling is performed efficiently under updates, we 553 can have a dynamic algorithm for approximate necklace splitting with an update time that 554 only depends logarithmically on m. Indeed, assume that the tree Tis constructed in the 555 preprocessing phase. It is known that a red–black tree can be updated in O(logm)time under 556 insertion/deletion of an element. Thus, our algorithm for the dynamic necklace splitting 557 problem consists of maintaining Tunder relocations/insertions/deletions (a relocation can 558 be handled as a deletion followed by an insertion). When the user requests the set of cuts, 559 we execute ApproxStatic as a subroutine using the updated T. We will henceforth refer to 560 this procedure as Approx. 561 When a batch of kupdates is encountered, Tis updated in O(klogm)time, and the 562 new set of cuts can be constructed in O/parenleftbig k322kε−2(logm)2/parenrightbig time.
